<!--# 1. Why did you do it? (What is the problem you have tackled and why is it important? 50 words) -->
<!--# Land use changes impact stream ecosystems through overland and subsurface flow paths connecting catchments to streams. Past studies have shown near-stream forest and hydrologically-efficient surfaces exert greater influence on in-stream macroinvertebrate assemblages than more distant cover. In the Naarm/Greater Melbourne region, the availability of high-resolution headwater stream mapping, finer-grained forest and impervious cover data, and joint-taxon modelling approaches permits review of past studies by evaluating the effect of improved data and methods on past conclusions. -->

Land-use changes impact stream ecosystems through flow paths from their catchments, with greater impact from near-stream, and efficiently drained land. New high-resolution stream and land-use data for the Naarm/Melbourne region and joint-taxon modelling approaches allow review of past studies that have contributed to this understanding of land-use effects.

<!--#  2. What did you do? (Outline the methods you used, 50 words) -->
<!--# We fitted hierarchical linear models to joint macroinvertebrate taxon presence-absence and to Stream Invertebrate Grade Number Average Level (SIGNAL) in response to 7 environmental variables including exponentially weighted forest cover and impervious cover. Using first a new high-resolution stream network, and then the network pruned to a similar density to a past study in the same region, we identified the optimal weighted forest cover by comparing the plausibility and Pseudo-Bayesian Model Averages of models with varying upstream flow ($W$) and overland ($L$) half-decay distances (HDD) for both EI and AF, and non-sampleable upstream flow ($sW$) for EI models. -->

We fitted hierarchical linear models to joint macroinvertebrate family presence-absence and to a biotic index (SIGNAL) in response to 7 environmental variables including exponentially weighted forest cover (AF) and impervious cover (EI). Using first a new high-resolution stream network, and then a pruned network similar to a past study, we identified optimal in-stream (W) and overland (L) half-decay distance (HDD) weightings for AF and EI, and HDD along small streams (sW) for EI.

<!--# 3. What were the results? (Focus on the key outcomes, 50 words) -->
<!--# The optimal predictor set for modeling macroinvertebrate assemblages included number of riffles, weighted forest cover, weighted imperviousness, mean annual rainfall runoff, catchment area, temperature, and degree of upstream regulation. SIGNAL score models performed worse when using the full stream network than the pruned mapping. Multi-taxon models fitted with AF variants performed equally well with either stream network. Weighting EI by $sW$ and $L$ improved multi-taxon model performance, but $W$ did not improve performance. The optimal AF weightings from multi-taxon models were $L = 5$ m (plausible range $0 < L < 32$ when $W > 600$, narrower than the 35 m determined in the past study) and $W = 633$ m (plausible range $200 < W < 1600$ when $L < 16$), and for EI weightings, $L = 44$ m (plausible range $2 < L < 128$ when $sW > 800$) and $sW = 1942$ m (plausible range $sW > 400$ when $L > 32$). -->

SIGNAL score models generally performed worse when using the full stream network than the pruned mapping. Multi-taxon models fitted with AF variants performed equally well with either stream network. Weighting EI by sW and L, but not W, improved the performance of multi-taxon models. Optimal attenuation lengths for AF from multi-taxon models were $L = 5$ m (plausible range $0 < L < 32$ when $W > 600$, narrower than the 35 m determined in the past study) and $W = 633$ m (plausible range $200 < W < 1600$ when $L < 16$), and for EI weightings, $L = 44$ m (plausible range $2 < L < 128$ when $sW > 800$) and $sW = 1942$ m (plausible range $sW > 400$ when $L > 32$).

<!--# 4. What do the results mean in theory? (What does your paper contribute to broader understanding? How will your results and conclusions change how people see the world? 50 words) -->

This suggests that the extent of stream network maps can influence the inferred effects of overland forest cover on stream ecosystems, and reveals in-stream-weighted effects that may not be detected without detailed headwater mapping.

<!--# 5. What do the results mean in practice? (What are the consequences of your work? How might your results and conclusions change what people do? 50 words) -->

Our analysis highlights that narrower riparian buffers (than previously inferred) can protect in-stream biota from land-clearance impacts. We also found wider buffers for impervious cover are needed to protect stream ecosystems, while emphasizing the importance of up-stream flow along small tributaries and headwater streams that were unmapped in the earlier study.
